## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# The Drawer That Stuck

The first thing I took to the repair café was a toaster that worked. I had misunderstood the sign. It said BRING SOMETHING BROKEN, but underneath, in smaller letters, it said OR COME FOR TEA. I read this as a loophole so conspicuous it must be a test. I put the toaster in a shopping bag and carried it six blocks.

“What’s wrong with it?” asked a woman named Ruth.

“Sometimes the toast comes out a little uneven.”

“What kind of bread?”

I told her.

“Oh,” she said. “That bread is always doing that.”

She gave me a cup of tea.

The café met on Saturdays in the basement of a church. There were long tables, an urn that made a convincing imitation of distant traffic, and a row of extension cords taped to the floor. The volunteers wore name tags with their specialties written beneath their names. RUTH — ELECTRICAL. GUS — WOOD. NADIA — SEWING. One man’s tag said PETER — PATIENT. He was sorting screws.

I had moved to the neighborhood in January. By April I knew which grocery store sold good apples and which bus driver would wait if you ran. These were useful things to know. I did not yet know anybody well enough to ask them to help me carry something upstairs.

At the next table, a boy had brought in a clock shaped like a cat. Its tail was supposed to swing. Ruth removed the back and asked him to hold the screws. After a while she asked him to hold the spring. He took both assignments seriously, but when she asked him what time he wanted her to set it to, he said, “Six.”

It was eleven in the morning.

“Six is when my dad gets home,” he explained.

Ruth set it to the actual time. “That way you’ll know how long you’ve got.”

The following Saturday I brought a drawer. It came from a little pine desk that had belonged to my father. You could open it if you pulled hard with both hands, but then it came all the way out and hit you in the stomach. My father had dealt with this by keeping things he rarely needed in it: spare shoelaces, old passports, the manual for a radio he no longer owned. When I inherited the desk, I added my own expired passport and pushed the drawer shut.

Gus turned it upside down. “Where’s the rest of it?”

“At home.”

“I can’t tell why it sticks without seeing what it sticks to.”

I had been hoping this would be the kind of repair that took ten minutes. The desk was up two flights of stairs, and the last time I’d moved it, my father had been at the other end. We’d both insisted on walking backward so the other one could see where he was going. We made it as far as the landing before realizing that wasn’t possible.

“I’ll bring it next week,” I said.

Peter, who was eating a biscuit over a tray of washers, asked how far away I lived.

“Six blocks.”

“Have you got stairs?”

“Yes.”

He picked up another biscuit for the road.

We got the desk downstairs by taking the drawers out and carrying it on its side. Peter went first. At the landing he set his end down and studied a crescent-shaped dent in the wall.

“That from the desk?”

“Yes.”

“Must have been coming up, then. We’re doing beautifully.”

Outside, we stopped twice. The first time was because Peter wanted to change his grip. The second was because a woman walking a small dog asked how much we wanted for the desk. Peter looked at me. I said it wasn’t for sale.

“Everything’s for sale,” she said, not aggressively. She had already leaned down to untangle the dog’s lead from a parking meter. “But you don’t have to sell it to me.”

By the time we got back, somebody had put the drawer behind the tea urn. Gus fetched it, slid it halfway into the desk, and pressed down on one corner. Then he took it out, rubbed chalk along the sides, and slid it in again. A little patch of chalk had rubbed off near the back.

“Here,” he said.

I put my finger where he pointed. The wood felt no different there than anywhere else.

Gus took two curls off the drawer with a hand plane and tried it again. It went all the way in. He opened it with one finger hooked around the knob.

“That’s it?” I asked.

“Want me to put it back?”

He showed me how to rub a candle along the runners. I did one side and he did the other. When we turned the drawer over, a photograph dropped from the narrow space behind its front panel. It showed my father at a picnic table, holding half an orange. Somebody just outside the frame had evidently asked him a question, because his mouth was open and his eyebrows were up. I turned the picture over. On the back he’d written a phone number without a name.

I waited for some more information to occur to me. None did. I put the photograph in my pocket.

Peter and I carried the desk home. At my door I asked if he wanted to come in for coffee. He said he’d already had enough tea to hear his own pulse, but he came in anyway. I had two chairs, one of which wobbled. He sat in that one and wedged a folded envelope under its short leg.

“You could bring that in,” he said.

“I could.”

“Or you could leave the envelope.”

After he went home, I opened the drawer a few times. If I pulled it with the old amount of force, it still came out and hit me. I had to learn to use less.

For a while I kept the photograph on top of the desk. Later I put it in the drawer with the passports. I thought I might forget it was there, but the drawer turned out to be a good place for things I needed all the time: scissors, tape, the little screwdriver that fits the screws in my glasses. I see the photograph most days now. Sometimes I take it out. More often I just move it aside to get at something underneath.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet, literary story uses a repair café and a stuck drawer to frame a newcomer’s gradual entry into community and memory.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant, dryly funny, and tender without insisting on a grand emotional revelation. Its pathos sits in practical details: the desk carried with the father, the photograph with no name attached, and the narrator’s admission that they do not yet know anyone well enough to ask for help. The reader is invited to notice how care can arrive as ordinary, shared work—and how learning to pull the drawer with less force echoes learning to live with what cannot be fully repaired or explained.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds small acts of help, the awkwardness of arriving somewhere new, inherited objects, and the limits of what memory can recover. Tea, tools, stairs, a wobbling chair, and the drawer recur as concrete forms of connection; the moral emphasis is on making room for one another without demanding a neat resolution.

## Evidence line
> I had moved to the neighborhood in January.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring objects and restrained emotional resolution make its chosen attention distinctive and coherent, while the evidence is concentrated in one carefully shaped narrative.
